content: Mefloquine is one of the four commonly recommended antimalarial drugs for travelers visiting malaria-endemic regions. Despite its high efficacy in preventing malaria, concerns have been raised regarding its psychological side effects. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of mefloquine as a prophylactic agent for malaria, a systematic review was conducted. This review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized cohort studies. The studies compared mefloquine with placebo, no treatment, or alternative antimalarial agents such as atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline. The populations studied included adults, children, and pregnant women. The review included 20 RCTs with 11,470 participants, 35 cohort studies with 198,493 participants, and four large retrospective analyses of health records involving 800,652 participants. Notably, nine RCTs excluded individuals with a history of psychiatric conditions, and 25 cohort studies selected antimalarial agents based on medical history and personal preference. Most studies relied on self-reported or clinician-assessed symptoms rather than formal medical diagnoses. Efficacy of Mefloquine In 12 trials comparing mefloquine with placebo, none were conducted in short-term international travelers, and most participants had some degree of malaria immunity. The incidence of malaria in the control group ranged from 1% to 82% (median 22%), while in the mefloquine group, it ranged from 0% to 13% (median 1%). In four RCTs involving non-immune, short-term international travelers, only one clinical case of malaria was reported among 1,822 participants. Safety of Mefloquine Compared to Atovaquone-Proguanil Participants taking mefloquine were more likely to discontinue the medication due to adverse effects compared to those taking atovaquone-proguanil (risk ratio [RR] 2.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.53 to 5.31; high-certainty evidence). Serious adverse effects were rare, with 15 cases reported among 2,651 mefloquine users and none among 940 atovaquone-proguanil users. In one RCT involving short-term travelers, mefloquine users were more likely to report abnormal dreams (RR 2.04, 95% CI 1.37 to 3.04; moderate-certainty evidence), insomnia (RR 4.42, 95% CI 2.56 to 7.64; moderate-certainty evidence), anxiety (RR 6.12, 95% CI 1.82 to 20.66; moderate-certainty evidence), and depressed mood (RR 5.78, 95% CI 1.71 to 19.61; moderate-certainty evidence). Cohort studies involving long-term travelers supported these findings, often with larger effect sizes. Mefloquine users also reported higher rates of nausea and dizziness (high-certainty evidence). The estimated absolute effect sizes for mefloquine versus atovaquone-proguanil were as follows: Discontinuation of the drug: 6% versus 2% Insomnia: 13% versus 3% Abnormal dreams: 14% versus 7% Anxiety: 6% versus 1% Depressed mood: 6% versus 1% Safety of Mefloquine Compared to Doxycycline No significant differences were observed in the rates of serious adverse effects between mefloquine and doxycycline users (low-certainty evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the rates of discontinuation due to adverse effects (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.87; low-certainty evidence). Mefloquine users were more likely to report abnormal dreams (RR 10.49, 95% CI 3.79 to 29.10; very low-certainty evidence), insomnia (RR 4.14, 95% CI 1.19 to 14.44; very low-certainty evidence), anxiety (RR 18.04, 95% CI 9.32 to 34.93; very low-certainty evidence), and depressed mood (RR 11.43, 95% CI 5.21 to 25.07; very low-certainty evidence). These findings were consistent across cohort studies involving long-term travelers, but one RCT in military personnel did not show differences in the frequency of abnormal dreams or insomnia between groups. Mefloquine users were less likely to report the following adverse effects compared to doxycycline users: Dyspepsia (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.74; low-certainty evidence) Photosensitivity (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.11; very low-certainty evidence) Vomiting (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.27; very low-certainty evidence) Vaginal thrush (RR 0.10, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.16; very low-certainty evidence) The estimated absolute effect sizes for mefloquine versus doxycycline were as follows: Discontinuation: 2% versus 2% Insomnia: 12% versus 3% Abnormal dreams: 31% versus 3% Anxiety: 18% versus 1% Depressed mood: 11% versus 1% Dyspepsia: 4% versus 14% Photosensitivity: 2% versus 19% Vomiting: 1% versus 5% Vaginal thrush: 2% versus 16% Additional Findings Comparisons of mefloquine with chloroquine did not provide new information. Subgroup analyses based on study design, travel duration, and military versus non-military participants yielded no conclusive results. Conclusions The absolute risk of malaria during short-term travel is low with all three established antimalarial agents: mefloquine, doxycycline, and atovaquone-proguanil. The choice of antimalarial agent should be guided by individual preferences regarding specific adverse effects, pill burden, and cost. While some travelers may prefer mefloquine for its once-weekly dosing schedule, this must be weighed against the increased likelihood of experiencing abnormal dreams, anxiety, insomnia, and depressed mood.
